Title: 🍂 Autumn Activity Weeks - Metroland Meets the Chilterns
Summary:
🍂 This event is part of our
Autumn Activity Weeks
— get active, get social and get out more!
Beauty Sleep:
⏰ Bonus lie-in alert! This walk takes place on the first day of GMT, so the clocks go back and you get an extra hour in bed beforehand. Enjoy it — but don’t forget to set your alarm and join us on time for the adventure! The downside is that it will be getting darker earlier in the evenings!
Overview:
Leave the Metropolitan line behind and swap the city for a fine Chilterns autumn hike. From Amersham Station we'll first navigate towards Old Amersham, with its colourful and historic High Street before heading out into a landscape of rolling hills, woodland and small villages, when hopefully late October will be putting on quite a show.
After a steady ascent out of Old Amersham, with views across the Misbourne Valley and a number of fields to traverse, later our route winds through the magnificent Hodgemoor Woods, passes the pretty hamlets of Winchmore Hill (where we will stop for lunch) and Penn Street, and follows a network of leafy paths, quiet lanes and open countryside that's made for crisp autumn walking. Expect crunchy leaves underfoot, woodland colours at their best and plenty of opportunities to stop for those obligatory "look at that tree!" moments.
Towards the end we'll stroll back through the historic High Street of Old Amersham, with its timber-framed buildings and coaching inns, and drop into one of the pubs for a late afternoon drink before one further mile and one final uphill climb back to the station.
At
11.8 miles
with around
300 metres of ascent
, this is a moderately challenging walk with enough hills to earn your lunch, plenty of beautiful scenery to distract you from them, and, as always, great company throughout.
The Route:
The route can be found
here
:
The Sites:
Metroland:
is the name given to the leafy suburbs and towns that grew up along London's Metropolitan Railway in the early 20th century, promoted as offering the perfect balance of country living and an easy commute into the capital. Amersham marks the northern edge of this historic "Metroland", where the suburban landscape gives way to the rolling hills, ancient beech woodlands and picturesque villages of the Chilterns, making it the ideal gateway from town to countryside.
Amersham-On-The-Hill & Old Amersham:
The town has two distinct parts set apart from one another. Amersham-on-the-Hill grew with the arrival of the Metropolitan Railway in the early 20th century and became part of the commuter belt. Old Amersham is the historic heart of Amersham, centred on a beautifully preserved High Street lined with timber-framed buildings, Georgian townhouses and traditional coaching inns. Once an important stop on the main London to Aylesbury route, it retains much of its medieval character, with landmarks including the historic Market Hall and the impressive St Mary's Church, parts of which date back to the 13th century. Today, its bijou independent shops, cafés and pubs make it one of the Chilterns' most attractive market towns.
Hodgemoor Woods:
has ancient beech, oak and hornbeam trees which if we are lucky with autumn colours turn into a display of gold, copper and russet colours.
Winchmore Hill:
is a small English village with a village green.
Penn Street:
is a hamlet village surrounded by rolling hills, ancient woodland and some of the finest countryside in Buckinghamshire.
Dogs:
Well-behaved dogs are welcome, there will be a few areas where we are walking along or crossing roads but the majority of the walk is in open countryside where dogs can be let off the lead. Please abide by the Countryside Code (
https://tinyurl.com/rlqvp3h
) and remember not everyone loves dogs as much as you do so be mindful of other members.
Photos:
All photos the leader's own (taken in Sept 2026), with permission given to OutdoorLads for use.
Difficulty & Distance: 11.8 miles, good condition paths of grass, dirt and tarmac, moderately undulating with a total ascent of 300 meters

Title: European Snow Pride 2027
Summary:
EUROPEAN SNOW PRIDE 2027 - 20-27 MARCH in Tignes
***
European Snow Pride booking is now  open
!! ***
This event is intended to to provide information about snow pride and facilitate (primary via the WhatsApp group) people arranging to share accommodation prior to the event as well as communication on the event.
There is a social organised for the second evening to meet other Outdoorlads whilst there.
However most of the socialising is via the snowpride ski groups and parties and not specifically organised with Outdoorlads as you may have experienced on a typical Outdoorlads event.
This is EUROPE'S BIGGEST GAY FESTIVAL OF  WINTER SPORT & MUSIC with guests coming from all over Europe, North America and beyond.
It takes place in the gay friendly resort of TIGNES and in the snow sure and huge beautiful ski area of Tignes and Val D'Isere!
European Snow Pride features great apres ski on the slopes, with DJs, singers and performers, Fantastic club parties including a giant pool party, a gay pride parade and much more.
A unique opportunity to meet people from all around the world and make new friends!
If you have not attended one of these type of events before they are great fun. In the daytime there are guided groups that you can join for skiing or snowboarding where you will meet lots of other gay guys, and rendezvous restaurants where multiple groups meet for lunch. In the evening there are parties every nite some are themed (fancy dress) and are great fun. In between there is apres ski at the end of the day and the spa (if you have access) .
For more info:-
European Snow Pride website
.
European Snow Pride on facebook
.
PLEASE NOTE THERE ARE TWO EUROPEAN SKIING EVENTS THIS ONE, (EUROPEAN SNOW PRIDE ESP) AND EUROPEAN GAY SKI WEEK  EGSW SO MAKE SURE YOU ARE SIGNING UP TO THE ONE YOU WANT TO ATTEND , ESPECIALLY IF YOUR FRIENDS ARE BOOKED ON ONE. THIS EVENT IS FOR EUROPEAN SNOW PRIDE in TIGNES
There is a WhatsApp group to assist people in communicating to book / share accommodation and to communicate and arrange to meet up whilst there. See the link in the location information below to join.
Please read the info on here carefully and on the ESP website, feel free to ask questions in the whatsapp group.
ACCOMMODATION
There are lots of options see the
European Snow Pride website
for details.
When booking for accommodation is open. I recommend booking ASAP as the best accommodation offers sell out early and the cost increases a little every month !
There are the special offer accoms ranging from approx £500 to £800 these are already really good value as this also includes the event pass and lift pass.
You will need to pay 25% on booking and the remainder 1 month before the event.
I will be booking the deluxe special offer (£798pp (increases monthly)), a lot of the outdoorlads book this as is really good value and it makes shareing with other outdoorlads simple. The apartments are great, it is close to the slopes and it has access to the fantastic spa. This includes both event and lift passes. So just flights, transfers and spending money on top.
The deluxe secial apartments are for 5 people but you don't need to arrange who you are sharing with till later so I recommend booking to secure a place as this will sell out. (There are lots of other options and the non special offer accom is eligible for a small discount see
ODL Discount
). If you are on a tight budget the standard special is great value at £517.
(shareing a small apartment with 4) There is also a comfort special (shareing with 3).
If you have got your own group together then great , if not message on the WhatsApp group , see link in the location information below to join the group, ask if any other outdoorlads are looking to share. With the special offer accom , snowpride will allocate you an apartment with others you request to share with and/or will fill spaces with others on snowpride.
I have shared with others i didn't know in the past and found it a great way to make new friends.
SKIING/SNOWBOARDING
There are daily guided groups for intermediate and advanced skiers/boarders and ski school available for beginners. This year each guided group will be accompanied by an ESP promoter and a professional ski guide from evolution 2.
European Snow Pride Ski options
.
You can hire  your equipment  from ESP also.
EVENT PASS ETC
To participate in the ski groups, a client must either purchase an Event Pass Premium, or an Event Pass Standard plus a supplement for ski and snowboard groups.
The standard includes the evening parties but not the daytime guided ski groups or the pool party.
This makes it more flexible so that if you do not use the guided ski groups or go to the pool party it will be cheaper for you. You can add the pool party or the guided groups to the Standard pass as an optional extra.
If you are intending to do the guided ski groups and pool party then it is more cost effective to get the premium.
Full details on the types of event pass here;:
https://www.europeansnowpride.com/fr/pass-evenement-gay-ski-week/

You need to organise your own transport .
See
European Snow Pride travel options

When booking flights to the resort the transfers usually leave the airports before 3pm on Saturday and are not likely to arrive back at the airport until after 3pm on the return journey. So please bear this in mind when booking flights. (As in, early flight on arrival and late flight on return. There have been many occasions with a late return transfer as Saturday is change over day for the whole of the french alps! The traffic is usually extremely congested, do not be misled by google travel times that are not for Saturday! Several people have missed flights booked too early in the day.)

Title: SE500 Golden Autumn in Goring - a two part walk
Summary:
A walk including the glorious colours of autumn through fine woodlands, as well as taking in the best of the vistas of the Thames Valley from grassy hilltops above Goring. Take the challenge of 500 metres of ascent over the walk, or choose half of it if you prefer a more gentle ramble!
This is a 2-part walk:
Part 1 – East of Goring: 12.2km with 269m of ascent with gentler slopes and woods.
Part 2 – West of Goring: 7.1km with 273m of ascent, including steeper slopes and open views.
Total: 19.3km and 542m of ascent.
You can choose at the end of Part 1 whether to continue with Part 2 or complete your walk at the station.
Meeting at Goring and Streatley Station, the morning walk takes in several attractive woodlands and views over farmland from the east of Goring. The rolling hills take the Chiltern Way, which we follow to start with, up over attractive rises giving good vistas west and south across the Thames valley. The morning walk consists of gentler slopes over a longer distance of 12.2km and 269m ascent.
Returning to Goring, Mill Cottage on the right can be seen. This was the house of musician George Michael. The village church is dedicated to St Thomas Becket and dates from the early 13th century.
There is an 18th-century coaching Inn, the Miller of Mansfield, as well as a couple of cafes and several small shops. We shall take lunch here, so you can choose to bring your own and use the benches in Rectory Garden, or get some food in the Inn, cafes, or buy from the shops.
At this point, you will have completed 12.2km. You have the option of continuing your walk to achieve the accolade of completing an SE500, or gracefully bowing out to return to the station, which is a stone's throw away.
After lunch, our walk takes us through the village and across the Thames bridge to the west bank. Originally a ferry, a wooden bridge was first built in 1837, and the weirs form an attractive backdrop. On the west side, the land rises steeply over the grassy slopes of Lardon Chase to the top of Lough Down hill (138m). This is a Site of Special Scientific Interest and has been preserved by the National Trust. Chalk-loving plants have been encouraged, and the slopes support a wide range of flowers and butterflies.
There is then a descent and ascent by a golf course and up into Common Wood. In clearings on the top are three labyrinth mazes formed by shallow mounds of earth and grass. The woods themselves include traditional oaks and chestnut.
Descending back to Goring station after completing the afternoon's 7.1km and 273m of ascent, you have achieved over 500m of ascent in total, over just over 19km - a great achievement helping to burn off around 2,100 calories!
Well behaved dogs are welcome on this walk. You can follow the
route
on OS Maps.

Title: An Illuminating Suppertime in Blackpool
Summary:
Join Andy and the OutdoorLads for a relaxed and enjoyable Friday evening supper in the heart of Blackpool!
This is a fun, friendly, and flexible social evening designed around whatever the group would most enjoy. Whether you're visiting Blackpool for the weekend's events that are running, or simply looking for an opportunity to meet new people, this promises to be a wonderful way to start the weekend.
We'll begin by taking a leisurely stroll along Blackpool's famous promenade, soaking up the lively atmosphere of one of Britain's most iconic seaside destinations. As we wander beside the coastline, there will be plenty of opportunities to chat, enjoy the sea views, watch the world go by, and admire the illuminations and attractions that make Blackpool such a vibrant place to visit.
After our walk, we'll head into town to find somewhere for a well-earned drink and supper. Blackpool's food scene has evolved dramatically in recent years, with a growing selection of restaurants, cafés, gastropubs, and independent eateries offering cuisine from around the world. From traditional favourites to exciting contemporary dining experiences, there is something to suit every taste and budget.
The evening is as much about the company as it is about the food. Sharing a meal together provides the perfect opportunity to relax, swap stories, make new friends, and enjoy the welcoming and inclusive atmosphere that OutdoorLads events are known for. Whether you're a regular attendee or joining us for the first time, you'll find a warm welcome and plenty of good conversation.
So come along and join us for a sociable evening of seaside strolling, great food, refreshing drinks, and excellent company as we discover some of Blackpool's newest and most exciting places to eat.
TRAVEL:
There are plenty of car parks in Blackpool, and there is free parking in the streets. A charge applies if you wish to park on the prom. Blackpool North and Blackpool South train stations are easily accessible. There are, of course, the trams which you can use.
DRESS CODE:
Smart casual clothing. No tracksuit bottoms please !

Title: Blackpool parkrun
Summary:
For those of you who enjoy your weekly parkrun fix, we'll be heading to
Blackpool parkrun
before the
Gay Illuminations Day Stroll
and
Blackpool Illuminations Social
later the same day. If you've not heard of it, parkrun is a free, weekly, timed 5k event that takes place every Saturday at locations across the world.
We will meet at 8.45am by the parkrun sign for a group photo. I'll be wearing a red parkrun t-shirt, and you're welcome to wear any OutdoorLads merchandise. You can register for parkrun and get your own barcode from
www.parkrun.org.uk
to scan at the end of your run to record your finish time if you wish. However, you do not need to do this to take part in the run if you don't want to.
Course description:
The course is 5k long, run on tarmac, gravel and trail paths. It’s an almost two lap, anti-clockwise course that is mainly flat. Some sections of the course may accumulate mud, leaves and puddles after rain.
The course starts on the tarmac path south of the clock tower between the netball courts and all weather football pitches. The actual start is parallel to the middle of three floodlights on the left. After the start the route takes the first path on the left. It then turns left adjacent to a black bin and passes by the BMX track which will be on your right. Follow the path towards the model village before exiting the park to turn left along the footpath of East Park Drive.
At the next entrance to the park we re-enter the park and make an immediate right turn onto the woodland trail which is twisty and in places narrow. We follow the lakeside shore for a while before making a right and left turn to take us away from the shore. Eventually the route re-joins the network of tarmac paths. Take the second path on the right and heads towards the crazy golf course. The course turns left here and makes a short descent to follow the Lakeside Promenade towards the bandstand.
The route goes left across the front of the bandstand and up the gravel slope on the right. Here it continues around on the first path to the right. When you catch sight of the rose garden on your left take the sharp turn to the left then turn sharp right to follow the right hand outer path of the rose garden with tennis courts on your right. At the pavillion turn right towards the clock tower. At the clock tower turn left and cross the start line to commence the second lap which is the same as the first lap until you reach the rose garden for the second time. To finish you follow the centre path in the rose garden. The course ends in-between the first two bushes in the garden.
On occasion parkruns can be cancelled due to the weather or lack of volunteers. Should this happen I will try to contact members as soon as I can.

Title: The Wild Side of Welford: Field, Furrow & Towpath
Summary:
The ancient coaching village of
Welford
sits on the extreme edge of
Northamptonshire
– tight up against the border with
Leicestershire
.
Lying half way between Northampton and Leicester, Welford became an important resting place for stage coaches – at one time having seven Inns or Coaching Houses along the present High Street. These days, the village is very easily accessible - just a mile or so from junction 1 of the A14.
Our walk begins with arguably the stand-out selfie opportunity of the year. A chance to get a picture taken alongside
Postman Pat
and his black and white cat! During the meticulous research phase of preparing this walk(!), I couldn't find a reason why Pat and Jess are celebrated here in this way – especially since the postie's round is miles away in Cumbria! Anyway, let's not quibble – Welford is proud to celebrate these iconic characters and they've become a popular attraction.
Pat points the way to our first path which takes us around the periphery of the village before we head off across the fields to the
Grand Union Canal
.
Joining the towpath, we soon skirt around the site of the medieval village of
Downton
. Don't get too excited – the history of this village is largely unknown, having been completely deserted by the early 18th century. Both the canal construction and the modern mechanised plough have taken their toll. Spoiler alert: nothing remains!
We'll have just over 2 miles to enjoy this particularly tranquil stretch of the Grand Union Canal before we join a brief section of the
Jurassic Way
– a long distance path which connects Banbury in Oxfordshire with Stamford in Lincolnshire, largely following an ancient ridgeway traversing Britain.
This path takes us up into the
Hemplow Hills
and a beautiful wooded area. As we emerge from the trees, we'll pause for a picnic lunch.
A series of footpaths and bridleways take us east and then north until we hit the upper reaches of the
River Avon
. We're very close to the river's source near
Naseby
and so, at this point, the Avon is nothing more than a babbling brook. Hard to believe that after Rugby and Warwick, these waters flow through the iconic tourist scene at Stratford before running past Evesham to join the Severn near Tewkesbury.
We'll walk alongside the Avon across the final few fields before Postman Pat welcomes us back to
Welford
.
For those that want to stay on, we have the option to walk a couple of hundred yards through Welford's charming Pocket Park to cross over the border into Leicestershire and enjoy refreshments at the
Wharf Inn
.
Dogs are welcome:
Our walk includes field paths, bridleways, village streets and we cross one minor A road. We may encounter sheep, lambs, cows or horses and there are a few fields where landowner signs request dogs on a lead.

Title: 🍂 Autumn Activity Weeks - Chislehurst and its Caves: Daylight Shunned and Daylight Saved on My 300th Lead
Summary:
🍂 This event is part of our
Autumn Activity Weeks
— get active, get social and get out more!
As this event includes an exclusive guided
tour of Chislehurst Caves
, it is £13 for all members.
The clocks actually go back on Sunday 25th October, but creepy, chilly Chislehurst Caves couldn't take our booking for a guided tour then. The day that British Summer Time ended would have been so appropriate, because on the tour of the town and fields of Chislehurst that we'll do after our tour of the caves, we'll encounter the grave of the man who did most to bring about Daylight Saving, one William Willett. While out on the remarkably rural green spaces in between the handsome houses, we'll also encounter Malcolm Campbell, Napoleon III and Charles de Gaulle. The dwindling daylight of Autumn will be a motif of the walk, shunned in the caves, saved in the history and savoured on the heaths.
The sights:
Chislehurst:
A wooded, affluent suburb with medieval origins. Its historic core centres on the High Street and St Nicholas’s Church, whose churchyard contains the burials of William Willett, the advocate of daylight saving, and Sir Malcolm Campbell, the land- and water-speed record holder. The village expanded rapidly after the railway arrived in 1865, attracting substantial Victorian houses and wealthy City residents. We'll also glimpse Camden Place, the home of the French Emperor Napoleon III from 1871 to 1873. Napoleon staged a coup d’état in 1851 against Napoleon I's nephew, Louis-Napoleon, overthrowing the Second Republic's constitutional government, proclaiming himself Emperor Napoleon III and establishing the Second French Empire. Following personal defeat during the Franco-Prussian War at the Battle of Sedan in 1870, he was overthrown and the Third Republic was proclaimed. Captured by the Prussians, he went into exile in Britain, settling at Chislehurst, where he died in 1873. His Empress, Eugénie, lived on occasionally there, dying in 1920.
Chislehurst Caves
:
A 22-mile labyrinth of artificial chalk workings, excavated from the C18 onwards for chalk, lime and flint, the chalk was used agriculturally and the flint for firearm triggers. Opened as a visitor attraction in 1900, the atmospheric tunnels soon acquired legends and ghost stories, but their most important use came during the Second World War, when they became a vast deep air-raid shelter accommodating up to 15,000 people, some of whom continued to live underground after their homes had been destroyed. By November 1940, special evening trains ran from Cannon Street to Chislehurst to cope with the crowds. Hitler knew about them and Lord Haw-Haw referred to them, ominously warning that the Germans 'knew about the rats living underground in Kent' and that they 'were coming to get them'. Later used for mushroom cultivation and as a concert venue, with David Bowie, Pink Floyd and Jimi Hendrix performing there in the 1960s and 1970s. The carvings made by New Zealand-born artist Sandy Brown, who worked alone underground, and until 1985 a £5 challenge was offered to anyone willing to spend the night alone in the caves. One policeman succeeded by spending the night carving a figure into the wall, but afterwards said he would never repeat the experience, while another challenger was found unconscious and unable to explain what had happened. They were used as a filming location for
Doctor Who
’s 1972 serial
The Mutants
, in which the Third Doctor and Jo Grant help the Solonians overthrow the evil Marshal. We’re booked in for an exclusive 50-minute tour covering one mile, not 22!. See the video
here
.
Scadbury Park:
A rare survival of a medieval rural landscape within Greater London, encompassing woodland, meadows, farmland and historic parkland. Little-remains of the moated medieval manor house (foundations, cellars, undercroft, fishponds and traces of a bridge) which belonged to the Walsingham family from 1424, including Sir Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth I’s celebrated spymaster. Its ancient woodland, hedgerows and wetland habitats are of considerable ecological importance.
Petts Wood:
An inter-war garden suburb, developed after 1928. Detached and semi-detached houses, mature gardens and tree-lined streets. The adjoining woodland, protected from development by the National Trust, is central to its identity. Leader of the Free French and future President of France Charles de Gaulle and his family lived briefly at 41 Birchwood Road in 1940, during his wartime exile, before bombing prompted their move to Shropshire.
William Willett Memorial:
A 1927 memorial sundial to builder William Willett (1856-1915), who campaigned for daylight saving, stands in the woodland. Set to British Summer Time, it bears the apt inscription,
“I only tell the summer hours”.
Willett became Britain’s leading campaigner for daylight saving. The idea reportedly came to him during an early-morning ride near Petts Wood, when he noticed people sleeping despite the summer daylight. In 1907 he published
The Waste of Daylight
, proposing that clocks should advance progressively in spring and revert in autumn, allowing more evening daylight and reducing artificial-light consumption. Despite support from Winston Churchill, his proposals failed in Parliament. Willett died in 1915 without seeing them adopted. Britain introduced British Summer Time in 1916, partly to conserve coal during the First World War.
The
route
(please click to see it at the Ordnance Survey)
:
We'll walk along Station Approach to Old Hill before turning down Forest Close to go to the caves. Back on Old Hill, we'll walk to the Bromley Road, see Camden Place, then cross Chislehurst Common to Centre Common Road. We'll go up the High Street, turn right up Park Road, the take an alleyway to Foxbury, and go in a loop round to the Cemetery, cross the A222 and follow a footpath across Scadbury Park. We'll then follow the London Loop and Manor Park Road southwest to Chislehurst Church and the Tiger's Head. We'll then follow Hawkwood Lane and Botany Bay Lane before veering east to resume the London Loop, only leaving it to see Birchwood Road. Re-emerging into an open space, we'll follow Kyd Brook and Gosshill Road back to Station Approach.

Title: Festive Grandeur at Knightshayes Court
Summary:
Kick off the festive season with a scenic, varied winter day walk on the Devon/Somerset border! Starting directly from the National Trust’s grand
Knightshayes Court
estate, our circular route weaves together peaceful estate parkland, the River Exe valley, the historic Grand Western Canal, and quiet rolling country lanes through charming hamlets.
We’ll finish our hike back at Knightshayes with plenty of time in the afternoon to warm up with hot drinks, festive treats, and explore the spectacular Victorian Gothic mansion dressed in its full Christmas glory.
Event Overview
Duration:
~4 to 4.5 hours (excluding post-walk estate visit)
Distance:
~8.5 miles (13.5 km)
Difficulty:
Moderate. A mix of estate trails, flat canal towpath, gentle rural ascents, and quiet paved country lanes.
Pace:
Social and steady, with stops for photos and a packed lunch on the trail.
The Route Highlights
Knightshayes Parkland & Bolham:
Leaving the estate grounds, we head west through ancient parkland before dropping down towards the picturesque village of Bolham.
Grand Western Canal:
Joining the tranquil, flat towpath at the edge of Tiverton, following the historic waterway eastward toward Copplestone.
Devon Countryside & Hamlets:
Turning north through rolling countryside, passing Craze Lowman, Peadhill, and the village of Chevithorne before looping back through Chettiscombe.
Estate Return:
Entering the Knightshayes grounds through the tranquil wooded trails to complete the loop.
Afternoon: Knightshayes Christmas Festivities
After completing the walk, we will head into the courtyard to enjoy a well-deserved hot drink, mince pie, or festive treat from the Stables Café. You’ll then have the rest of the afternoon free to tour the
Knightshayes Victorian mansion
, lavishly decorated with towering Christmas trees, seasonal garlands, and glowing period displays.
Note: Access to the estate grounds and car park is free for National Trust members (remember to bring your NT card!). Non-members can pay for parking/entry on the day.
Dogs
Dogs are welcome to join us on this event but we do ask the following:
Please appreciate the fact that not everyone is a dog owner or lover- especially when we stop to eat
Please ensure you adhere to the Countryside Code at all times - see (
Keeping Dogs Under Effective Control)
If your dog is uncontrolled and strays in open land frightening other animals or livestock, the leader is supported by the OutdoorLads board of trustees to ask you to leave the event as this is not acceptable behaviour.
Please note that dogs are not allowed inside Knightshayes Mansion.
Photo Credits:
All photos taken by OutdoorLads Members and permission is granted to OutdoorLads for further use.
Also - please note:
All photos taken during summer.  Obviously in December it'll be a lot more wintery and less sunny!

Title: Frensham in Autumn
Summary:
Let’s make the most of an autumnal Sunday with a relaxed walk through some of Surrey’s loveliest heathland.
Starting at Shortfield Common, we’ll head towards the beautiful Frensham Great and Little Ponds, enjoying sandy heathland tracks, woodland and open views across the water.
We’ll take our time, enjoy the scenery and have plenty of opportunities for chats and laughs along the way. And, naturally, there’s a very good reason to keep walking to the end: The Holly Bush pub, where we can round things off with a well-earned drink.
A great autumn outing for Outdoor Lads — fresh air, beautiful countryside, good company and a pub at the finish. What’s not to like?

Title: Autumn Ayots and Shaw's Corner
Summary:
Join Alex for this 11-mile autumnal amble around assorted Ayots.
We will meet at Welwyn North station and head southwest into the village of Digswell, dominated by a large viaduct carrying the East Coast Mainline across the valley of the River Mimram. We will pass the parish church of St John the Evangelist and Digswell Hall before entering Sherrardspark Wood, a large nature reserve on the edge of Welwyn Garden City.
Here we will turn west through the small settlements of Ayot Green and Ayot Little Green and follow the Ayot Greenway, a disused railway line now used as a track for walkers and cyclists. We will skirt fields and woodlands as our route takes us northwest towards the village of Ayot St Lawrence.
On arrival in the village we will pass Shaw's Corner, the home of the playwright George Bernard Shaw, author of
Pygmalion
and
St Joan
, and recipient of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1925. We will stop for lunch in the classical church of St Lawrence built in 1778 as a replacement for the 12th-century original.
After lunch we will turn east, passing the ruins of the old church and heading out into more open countryside. Our route will take us through historic Welwyn, the original settlement of that name before the establishment of the much larger garden city in 1920, passing the parish church of St Mary the Virgin.
On leaving Welwyn we will cross more farmland and woodland before arriving back at at station, which has a convenient pub just next door.
Don't waste that space!

Title: Fantastic Finchale
Summary:
Our route follows the winding Wear in places, and old railway lines in others. We pass a number of disused pits that have now been turned into a park and a nature reserve. There are stretches that are more suburban, and some roadside walking, but I have tried to keep this to a minimum. There is a little bit of ascent on this route (under 200 metres) and the route includes good surfaces in the main.
This walk starts at
Finchale Priory
, an English Heritage site. There will be time to visit the priory on our return, in case you wish to get your history fix.  We initially head towards Great Lumley. After around 1 1/2 hours of the walk, you will start to get some views of
Lumley Castle
(sadly not home to Joanna!).  We skirt parts of the golf course, before getting a better view after passing through Lumley Thicks (woodlands).
We then follow a shaded path towards Bournmoor, and on to
Elba Park
, where you can see an interesting sculpture commemorating the Wooden Wagonway. We pass close to Fence Houses, before continuing on to the
Rainton Meadows Nature Reserve
.
We walk on and pass Leamside, before we take a short loop through Cocken Woods and reconnect with the River Wear, back to our starting point.
After the walk, there will be an opportunity for a drink at The Three Horseshoes, before we head home.

Title: Pendle Hill Halloween Walk
Summary:
On Halloween itself, the hill made famous by witchcraft, mist and mystery will cast its spell over the Ribble Valley and the Borough of Pendle on this atmospheric high-level circular walk. 💀
Halloween costumes are optional—but very welcome!  🎃
We’ll tackle the whaleback shape of Lancashire’s Pendle Hill from Barley, travelling via Newchurch-in-Pendle, home of the Demdike family of Pendle Witch fame. 🧙🏻‍♀️
From there, we’ll pass Fell Wood, overlooking the Ogden Reservoirs, before climbing through Ogden Clough and onto the Pendle Hill plateau.
We’ll follow the plateau clockwise along its north-western flanks, taking in sweeping views across the Ribble Valley and towards the Yorkshire Dales, before reaching the trig point at Big End. 🧟‍♂️
We’ll then descend through the farms of Pendle Side and Windy Harbour, pass Lower Black Moss Reservoir and return to Barley for a well-earned pint—
the perfect ending to a Halloween adventure
. 👻

Title: Historical Trefil and the Charterist Caves
Summary:
A varied and interesting route taking in a range of historical and culturally important locations against the backdrop of stunning views of the Bannau Brycheiniog.
Starting in Trefil -  at 409m the highest village in Wales - we follow the old Bryn Oer tram road north past the limestone quarries of the area. After a slight detour to the Duke's Table, we head to the other worldly abandoned North Quarry. This strange landscape is a favoured filming location and has appeared on many TV series and films, including Dr Who, Torchwood, Wrath of the Titans, Merlin and the Hitch Hiker’s Guide to the Galaxy. Here we will visit the curios Naughty Stone and take in the views down Duffryn Crawnon and across the Bannau Brycheiniog - described as one of the most beautiful views in Wales. This area was a favourite place of Aneurin 'Nye' Bevan - a former coal miner in the area, he became Minister of Health and spearheaded the creation of the National Health Service in 1948. He loved to roam in these hills and his ashes are scattered on this unique landscape.
We head back through the woods before heading across to Mynydd Llangynidr. Here we will be off the path and crossing open moorland taking in more sweeping views as we climb Garn Fach and then onto Garn Fawr - a large bronze age burial Cairn. From here we navigate across to Ogof Fawr  - more commonly known as Charterist Caves. We will gather at the mouth of the caves to learn about its role in the Charterist Uprising of 1839 and its role in modern British democracy. After we descend across a limestone landscape back to the eerie disused western quarry before heading back to the village for optional refreshments in the
Quarrymen's Arms
pub.
This is a great walk to get a feel of the wilderness of the Bannau Brycheiniog without committing to a long day in the hills, while learning how local communities have worked, lived and been inspired by the landscape.
The key constraint on participant numbers on this walk is parking, so if you can please try to.lift share to reduce the number of vehicles we take to the start point.
All pictures by
David Pugh
/
Caerphilly Adventure Group
and used with permission.
Difficulty & Distance: 14km walk and 300m of ascent in mixed terrain, with some climbing and crossing of open exposed moorland. Parts also pass through old quarries and limestone landscapes with uneven surfaces.

Title: Bannau Brycheiniog - the Fforest Fawr Fan Clwb
Summary:
Fforest Fawr is a UNESCO Global Geopark is set within the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park in south Wales. It sits to the West of the more famous central Beacons - it is less popular but no less dramatic than its neighbours. The peaks may not be as high but the views are just as spectacular, the routes as challenging and it benefits from being far quieter. The wild mountains and hidden valleys of the geopark are the result of nearly 500 million years of Earth history. This fascinating area contains evidence of ancient seas, mountain building and sea level and climate change scattered across a landscape that was shaped by the last ice age.
Parking at the quieter Craig Cerrig-gleisiad parking area we start by exploring this often overlooked Nature Reserve. It is a dramatic glacial cwm,  often nicknamed the "Eiger of the Beacons" for its steep, imposing north-facing cliffs. It is a haven for rare arctic-alpine plants and upland birds. We climb around the area to the peak of Fan Frynych (629) to take in the views across the whole Bannau Brycheiniog range. We then traverse across the top of the cliffs before crossing wild moorland to climb Fan Fawr (734) to take in views across to Corn Du and Pen y Fan  We descend down towards Storey Arms. Depending on conditions and time we will either heading back to the reserve via  Craig y Fro or along the Taff Trail.  This is a tough walk in places - the ascent and descent of Fan Fawr can be steep and the area can feel more remote and isolated than its busier neighbours. However we start gently with a good warm up on Fran Frynach and we are rewarded with experiencing the quiet wilderness of this special area.
There are excellent opportunities to try out your navigation skills on this walk - whatever your level. If you are interested in learning or practising any techniques on the day let me know beforehand.

and used with permission.

Title: Rugged and Romantic: the 'Lads, the Mens and some Studs
Summary:
The 'rugged and romantic' of the title applies (apart from to us and any strapping strangers we might meet) to the landscape which is some of the most hidden and hilly in West Sussex. Although possessing a topography unlike the sweeping South Downs, the area is part of that national park. The 'Lads' in the title might be obvious, but 'The Mens' is a wooded nature reserve with an untamed, uncanny feeling, its ancient trees soaring then falling and their hulks becoming a home to a myriad fungi. The area's remoteness includes from the masses, as its sturdy sandstone, tiled and timber-framed buildings house both the upper crust and their horses (the studs of the title) in equal luxury.
The sights:
The Mens:
The Sussex Wildlife Trust
website
says: 'A largely unex­plored wood, it certainly has an untamed, mysterious feeling to it and many people describe it as ‘wild’...A lack of management in recent years has added to this silvicultural diversity. As you start to wander through the reserve, you will begin to orientate yourself – there are old tracks and banks separating woodland compartments and heavily incised streams full of bryophytes that fracture and divide the site – old fallen giants are found everywhere, many...now home to important populations of saproxylic inverte­brates, fungi (almost 600 species found so far) and bats. Trees are almost always left as they have fallen and the amazing structure this creates adds to the wild feel.' The name is from the Anglo-Saxon ‘ge-mænnes’, meaning common land.
Crimbourne Farm:
A big half H-shaped house, rambling thanks to the accretions of many centuries from the C16 to the C19. Good barns all around in stone, tile and weatherboarding. Stables and stud farm adjacent. Set in one of the most picturesque landscapes in the county.
Stopham:
Just a simple church and a few cottages with superb countryside all around. St Mary's is C11 and C12 with a fine collection of memorial brasses to the local Bartelot family in the floor. Stopham Manor is a splendid stone farmhouse of the C16. Stopham Bridge from 1483 occupies an idyllic spot despite the new bridge being built almost alongside. The centre arch was raised in 1822.
Bedham:
Just a farm, a derelict Victorian chapel and school and some fine houses set high on a wooded sandstone ridge in some of the hilliest and most remote scenery in Sussex. The chapel was founded in 1880, and abandoned in 1959.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this one is well-suited to them as there are few fields of livestock. However, there will be some stiles and roads to cross. A dog off a lead must be obedient.
The
route
(click the link to see it at the Ordnance Survey website):
We'll get to Coombelands Lane using an alleyway then use it to go north past Pickhurst, where we'll pick up a bridleway to go to Pallingham Quay, heading west. We'll then use Horsebridge Hill to go north and northeast before turning west along Crimbourne Lane. We'll then turn south and follow the Serpent Trail across The Mens and Hammonds Wood to Bedham where we'll have lunch. At Bedham Lane we'll turn southeast and at Mockbeggars turn down a bridleway to Harwoods Green. There, we'll use Woodcote Lane to get to Stopham. Leaving Stopham, we'll walk beside the A283 on the footpath, cross old Stopham Bridge, go to the pub, then follow the Wey South Path heading northeast back to Coombelands Lane and the alleyway back to the station.

Title: Londinium, Lundenburh, Londres - London from the Romans to the Normans
Summary:
Over 1000 years separate the oldest feature on this walk (the Roman amphitheatre of 70 AD) from the most recent we'll survey (St Bartholomew's Church of 1123), and although we won't see two key sights as they charge for entry (the Tower of London and Bishopsgate Roman Baths), we’ll still visit all of the Square Mile's surviving remains. Almost all of Saxon London has disappeared, but its churches, street pattern and place-names survive alongside much more substantial Roman remains. If Saxon London is mostly erased, Roman London is mostly buried and Norman London is mostly fragmentary, all the remnants make for the quintessential City look of ancient juxtaposed with modern.
Timeline of Roman, Saxon and Norman London:
43 AD: Roman conquest of Britain under Emperor Claudius.
47–50: Londinium founded, becoming a major port and commercial centre.
60–61: Boudica's rebellion: Londinium is burned and largely destroyed.
c. 70: London rebuilt; Roman amphitheatre constructed at Guildhall, initially in timber.
c. 100: Londinium reaches its greatest Roman prosperity.
120: Hadrian visits; amphitheatre rebuilt in stone; baths and temples built.
120–150: Cripplegate Roman fort built; London reaches its Roman peak.
120–130: Fire devastates much of Londinium; the city is rebuilt.
190–225: London Wall constructed, enclosing the main city.
240: Mithraeum built beside the Walbrook.
250–275: Riverside wall completes the enclosure of the city.
286–296: Carausius and Allectus overthrow Roman rule in Britannia.
296: Emperor Constantius Chlorus invades and re-establishes imperial control.
313: Christianity officially tolerated throughout the Roman Empire.
350: Towers added to London Wall as Saxon raids threaten.
400-410: Emperor Honorius gradually abandons Britannia. Londinium declines.
C5–C6: Roman London largely abandoned; the walls become ruinous.
C7: Anglo-Saxon trading centre Lundenwic develops where the Strand is.
886: King Alfred refortifies London within the Roman walls (Lundenburh).
994: Vikings under Sweyn Forkbeard begin raids.
1012: St Alphege murdered by Vikings; commemorated by St Alphege church.
1013: Sweyn captures London; King Æthelred forced to flee abroad.
1014: Æthelred (assisted by King Olaf) regains control.
1016: King Cnut the Great of Denmark conquers England.
1042: King Edward the Confessor re-establishes Saxon monarchy.
1042-1065: Edward the Confessor builds Westminster Abbey.
1066: William the Conqueror invades and is crowned at Westminster Abbey.
1066: William allows London to govern itself.
1070–1100: White Tower built, and completed in stone under William II.
1080: Undercroft and original church of St Mary-le-Bow.
C11–C12: Norman London expands within the Roman walls; defences repaired.
1123: Rahere founds St Bartholomew's Hospital and Priory.
c.1150: Norman London established as England's capital and mercantile centre.
The
route
and sights:
Starting at Bank Underground Station, we'll go up Princes Street, then west along Lothbury and Gresham Street and turn right into...
1.
Guildhall Yard and Guildhall Art Gallery: amphitheatre
.
The Yard uses a dark grey ring to preserve the outline of London's Roman amphitheatre, built 74 AD in wood, 31 years after the Roman conquest. Subsequently enlarged, including in 120 AD when it was rebuilt in stone. The enlarged version could hold 6,000 spectators, over a quarter of the population. Spectators would watch displays of gladiatorial combat, animals fighting and criminals being executed. A vertically sliding wooden door, possibly to allow animals to enter, has been carbon-dated. The present Guildhall is medieval, with the Great Hall dating from 1411, but the site has much older associations. The word
guildhall
derives from the Anglo-Saxon
gild
. (Note to self: booking is for 12.00.)
We'll then leave Guildhall Yard by its western side, and follow Love Lane and Oat Lane to Noble Street to see...
2. Noble Street Gardens:
Contains a substantial surviving section of London's Roman and medieval City Wall, incorporated into a small modern garden. The ancient Roman foundations were revealed when bomb damage from the Blitz was being cleared, revealing a fort in the northwest corner of the Roman walls (Cripplegate Fort) that had a garrison of 1000 soldiers and predates the wall.
We'll then continue from Noble Street on to London Wall, then go round the Rotunda and south down St Martins-Le-Grand to then cross Postman's Park heading west to Little Britain which we'll go up towards Cloth Fair where we'll find...
3. Church of St Bartholomew the Great:
Founded in 1123 by Rahere, courtier to Henry I as an Augustinian priory. Rahere was so distressed by the White Ship Disaster (which killed 300 people including Henry I's heir William Adelin, leading to The Anarchy) that he went on pilgrimage to Rome. Attributing his recovery from malaria to St Bartholomew, he founded a priory and a hospital in gratitude. St Bartholomew the Great is one of London's finest medieval survivors. Austere and dark but satisfying, its astonishing Norman fabric provides our walk's clearest architectural encounter with C12 London, and is the best example of Norman architecture outside of the Tower of London. Only the chancel remains, the nave destroyed by Henry VIII's wreckers.
We'll then follow Middle Street and Cloth Street to Aldgate. At The Rotunda we'll enter the Museum of London Car Park where we'll be astonished to find...
4. Fragment of the City Wall, Bay 52:
Just a small piece, but shows history erupting into the drab surroundings.
We'll emerge and proceed along London Wall, where we'll soon find...
5. City Wall Bastion 14:
Mostly medieval, not Roman, but it preserves the footprint and foundations of the earlier Roman defences. Illustrates exceptionally well the continuity and adaptation of London's defensive circuit.
Going into the Barbican Complex (itself named after the Roman Fort), we'll see...
6. Cripplegate Roman Fort Wall:
Dating from 120 AD. The tower is medieval.
Going along Monkwell Square and east along St Alphage Gardens, we'll find...
7. Roman Wall, Salters Garden:
Wall constructed AD 190–225. The Roman masonry here is now largely buried, having been truncated by later medieval rebuilding. Cripplegate Fort is buried beneath the northern wall here. The medieval wall is most of what shows here consisting of ragstone, flint and tile, with a battered outer face. The crenellations and brick diaper pattern is from 1477, added during the Wars of the Roses - the only surviving crenellations on the wall. St Alphage was the Archbishop of Canterbury, murdered by the Vikings in 1012 at Greenwich.
Emerging back on to London Wall (itself loosely following the Roman wall), we'll go east to Wormwood Street and then turn south down St Mary Axe to see...
6. Roman Girl's Grave, 30 St Mary Axe:
At the foot of the Gherkin is a memorial marking the grave of an unidentified Roman girl, 13-17 years old. Her remains were discovered during construction and date from approximately AD 350–400. It is one of the walk's most poignant sites: unlike the amphitheatre, baths and temples, a direct reminder of an individual who lived and died in Roman London.
Heading southeast down Brown's Buildings and Mitre Street, we'll go up St James's Passage to...
7. Aldgate Square:
By the medieval period, the city had outgrown the Roman wall that mostly defines the City of London. By the C18, the Roman gatehouses were is disrepair and impeded traffic, so like Ludgate, Cripplegate and others, Aldgate was pulled down, Aldgate in 1761. The church (1744, by George Dance the Elder) is St Botolph Without Aldgate, 'without' meaning outside of the city wall. St Botolph was a East Anglian saint associated with travellers, hence its location at an exit to the city when it was built originally in 1115. We'll have lunch in the gardens here.
We'll head south down Jewry Street, east down India Street and then turn right down Vine Street to...
8.
Vine Street Roman Wall
:
A substantial section of the city wall, together with the foundations of the only extant Roman bastion (375 AD) and later houses. This portion is in the basement of a modern building, carefully preserved and in 2023 made available for the public to view along with many historic objects. The surviving masonry also illustrates how Roman London continued to shape the medieval and modern city. We are booked in to view the wall and exhibition. (Note to self: booking is for 14.00.)
Continuing down Vine Street, we'll turn right down The Crescent to...
9. Roman Wall, Coopers Row:
A hidden but huge portion, 10.6 m high, although only the lower 6 m is Roman.
Emerging on to Trinity Square, we'll soon see more huge fragments of the Roman wall at...
10. Roman Wall, Wakefield Gardens:
One of the most substantial portions remaining. Most of the building above the red tiles is medieval. The statue is of the Emperor Trajan (ruled 98-117 AD) - a strange choice as he never visited the city unlike his adopted son and first cousin Hadrian.
Then, going under Tower Hill, we'll emerge at...
11. The Tower of London:
William the Conqueror began the White Tower around 1078, transforming this part of the eastern City into a major Norman royal fortress consolidating his power at the corner of the Roman fortifications and the growing mercantile centre. His son, William Rufus (William II) completed the rebuilding of the White Tower in stone. The most important Norman remains on the walk (the chapel of St John the Evangelist is sublime) charges £37 and we won't have time.
We'll walk around the Tower's western side towards Tower Hill, then continue north-west along Gloucester Court to...
12. All Hallows By The Tower:
The church is from the 1950s (by Lord Mottistone) to replace an earlier one destroyed in the Blitz, but the C14 undercroft contains a remarkable survival: a Roman mosaic pavement of a private house, and one what's more which is overlain with a replacement when the original became too wet. The pavement is 7 m below street level, illustrating the accumulation of detritus over time. The undercroft also contains a model of Roman London of 400 AD made in the 1920s. An exhibition of the history of Christianity in the city includes some C11 Saxon stone crosses - the only Saxon remains on the whole walk.
Going southwest down Byward Street and Lower Thames Street, we'll reach...
13. Billingsgate Roman House & Baths:
At 101 Lower Thames Street are the remains of a Roman house and bath complex, first constructed around AD 150. The baths were subsequently enlarged and used for several centuries. The surviving hypocaust illustrates the sophisticated underfloor heating technology of Roman London. Unfortunately, this charges £15 to enter and visiting is by guided tour only.
We'll then walk northwest up Monument Street, north up King William Street, west along Cannon Street, them up Walbrook to...
14. Forgotten Streams:
By sculptor Christina Iglesias, ‘Forgotten Streams’ is located at Bloomberg’s new European Headquarters. It evokes the lost rivers of London, namely the Walbrook along which the Romans built the Mithraeum, and the erasure of features and recycling of space in London.
Further up Walbrook is...
15.
London Mithraeum
:
Beneath Bloomberg's European headquarters is the London Mithraeum, a reconstructed Roman temple dedicated to the cult deity Mithras. The original temple was built in the C3 AD, beside the lost Walbrook River. The atmospheric reconstruction and associated archaeological displays make this one of London's best introductions to Roman religious life. (Note to self: booking is for 15.45.)
Going northwest up Bloomberg Arcade, then crossing Queen Victoria Street and proceeding up Watling Street, we'll turn right up Bow Lane and go through Bow Churchyard to go to...
16. St Mary-le-Bow:
Known for its bells, which feature in the nursery rhyme 'Oranges and Lemons', called back Dick Whittington in 1392 to become Lord Mayor, and define anyone born within earshot of them as true Londoner or Cockney. Wren's magnificent church of 1673 (tower finished 1680) is the third on the site. The earliest remains are a Norman undercroft of 1080. now a cafe.
Walking along Cheapside, we'll either go west to St Paul's or east to Bank Underground Stations to conclude our walk.
My many thanks go to ODL leader Alex Young for introducing me to the Guildhall amphitheatre, Vine Street Roman Wall and the Mithraeum on his excellent walks in the city, and letting me use his photos of the same.

Title: BIRMINGHAM Indoor Climbing - MONDAY - Beginners
Summary:
Join OutdoorLads for an evening at Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre.
*** Beginner (supervised) events are not offered every week ***
If you have never climbed before (or need a refresher on the basics), then this BEGINNERS EVENT is ideal for you! We will happily show you the ropes & teach you everything you need to know to climb safely!
Event pages are split into
BEGINNER & EXPERIENCED.
Please ensure you sign up to the correct event as we can only supervise two beginners at once per leader.
This event is for beginner climbers (those needing to be supervised) only!
If you are competent with how to tie in & belay (safely & confidently), then you will need to
sign up to the accompanying experienced (independent climber) event
instead.
If you are climbing with us for the first time, whether Experienced or Beginner, it is essential that you send a note to the Event Leader telling them about your previous climbing experience & your goals!
Bouldering
- Most of us do roped climbing, but if you prefer to do bouldering, you can sign yourself in & go bouldering (unsupervised) instead of, or as well as, roped climbing. Please meet the leader & the group at the start though; some others might wish to do bouldering too!
Please note that we will not teach lead climbing or lead belaying on this event -
we would suggest having some
lessons in Lead Climbing
by a qualified member of staff if this is something you're interested in pursuing!
If you are subsequently unable to attend, please cancel off the event. Spaces for beginners are limited & 'no-shows' are not only rude, but also frustrating for the leader & other attendees who may have travelled over an hour away to climb with you!
Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre
Indoor climbing centres offer the challenges of climbing that you'll find on natural rock crags - simply indoors! It's a fun way to stay fit, make new friends & develop your climbing skills.
Climbing
- Unlike Indoor Bouldering there is a certain amount of skill to be mastered, such as tying in knots & belaying a partner, as well as the climbs being higher than in bouldering. If you are new to climbing (or would like a refresher), there are plenty of top-rope routes to choose from after learning the essential climbing & safety techniques with one of our friendly, experienced climbing leaders.
Bouldering
- Instead of tackling long high routes, the 'problems' (as they are referred to) are shorter & focus on technique, balance, body positioning & sometimes power. With the different emphasis, bouldering doesn't have the hassle of climbing with ropes, so it’s excellent (but not necessarily easier) for newcomers.
Redpoint Birmingham Climbing Centre
has more than 75 lines with over 300 routes, set through some spectacular ground including its notorious 'stalactite'. It even features one of the few indoor 'Yorkshire VS cracks' in the country, to test your jamming skills. The bouldering rooms are just as interesting as its climbing routes, over 200 bouldering problems have been organised into graded circuits to provide something for everyone.

Title: Autumnal Weekend On The Slopes Of Skiddaw
Summary:
At 470m above sea level, Skiddaw House is the highest hostel in Britain. It was built around 1829 as a 'Keeper's lodge' and grouse shooting base for George Wyndham, the third Earl of Egremont. The building was originally divided into two separate dwellings; one side for the gamekeeper and his family and the other for a shepherd's family. The Earl and his shooting parties also had a few rooms to stay in when they came to visit. In 1986 the two dwellings were converted into the hostel it is today.
Skiddaw House operated as a youth hostel from 1987 until 2002, when it closed and began to fall into disrepair again. But with the help of the previous hostel manager, many volunteers and the Skiddaw House Foundation, the hostel was renovated and reopened in 2007. The building retains many original features, which combined with its interesting history and remote location make the hostel a unique place to stay.
One of the great features of Skiddaw House is its remote location, offering stunning views of the surrounding Lakeland fells. This venue is an OutdoorLads favourite and is truly special, right from the moment you park up you'll understand why this is so glorious!
However, the remote nature of the hostel means it is lacking the mod cons we may be used to, such as heating. Don't panic, there are a number of open fires throughout the building which helps keep it warm, but the bedrooms do not have any heating. Full bedding of 15tog duvets and pillow are provided but some may prefer to pack their own sleeping bag. Boots are also not allowed to be worn inside so we recommend packing slippers too!
Itinerary
Friday Afternoon/Evening -
Arrive at the car park for 15:00, meet the rest of the group and we will hike up to the hostel together,
sharing the load of weekend food supply bags
. Please have your head torch handy in case we start to lose the light! Once we have arrived and found our beds and settled in a bit, we'll have a briefing and dish out the traditional OutdoorLads buffet.
Important: If you're not able to arrive at the car park for 15:00, please message the event Leader at least a week before the event and we'll see what we can do. The walk in from the car park is over an hour long. Depending who signs up, we may be able to organise a second walk-in to the hostel with prior notice. There's no phone signal at the parking location or the venue. I'll share a route map from car park to hostel prior to the event in case of emergency.
Saturday Day -
A simple cold breakfast will be available. The main activity of the day will be a bit of a Wainwright epic, as we tick off up to 5 "Wainwrights," with the main attraction being Skiddaw (931m) on our hike. I expect we'll cover 14km in no more than 7 hours, with a total ascent of 1000m. However, if we're moving a bit slower or there is appetite to cut the walk short, we will be able to cut out some sections.
Saturday Evening -
Pop your feet up and unwind from the day's walk. We'll have a hearty evening meal to warm us back up, followed by some games and good laughs. While the hostel has a few, if you have a favourite travel size board/card game why not bring it?
Sunday -
Breakfast is provided once more then we'll all band together to tidy and clean up the hostel to how we found it (takes no time at all with so many) before we need to vacate by 11am. Once done we will take everything we brought back to the car park and then people might want to head home, or into Keswick for an afternoon touristing. I'll aim to lead a quick nip up to Blencathra (868m) via Hall's Fell Ridge, and back down to the car park. This is around 8km, 700m ascent, and should take around 4 hours.
Other information
Dogs:
The event leader very much welcomes well behaved, quiet dogs on this event. They should be able to cope with and enjoy a long mountain walk, be friendly with other dogs and people in a fairly small hostel, not go upstairs whilst wet, and be exceptionally well behaved around food. The venue has capped the number of dogs at three, and they and their humans will be assigned to one room, leaving other bedrooms available for humans only. Contact
support@outdoorlads.com
to reserve a dog space.
Food:
Please note that all food/drink provided will be plant-based. Whilst I encourage you all to embrace plant-based foods for the weekend, you are welcome to bring whatever buffet contributions you like. You'll also need to bring a packed lunch.
Skiddaw House requires a 1 hour hike to access it from the car park. To ensure everyone arrives safely we ask that all attendees meet at the car park for 3pm Friday so that we can hike up together. You will need to carry everything you need for the weekend including food and drink, plus a modest bag of supplies from the event leader in one trip - so pack light!

Difficulty & Distance: This hostel is aimed at mountain walking, and requires an hour hike carrying all your supplies plus an added bag, so a good level of fitness is needed

Title: 🍂 Autumn Activity Weeks - Gothic Ruins and Ghost Trains
Summary:
🍂 This event is part of our
Autumn Activity Weeks
— get active, get social and get out more!
Six hours or so hours after the witching hour (which is apparently between 3 and 4 in the morning) we'll start our walk. Our route to reach some Halloween hallmarks (castles, graveyards, relics) will proceed along trackways (or, if very muddy, quiet tarmac lanes) and go to West Grinstead, home to some vintage railway infrastructure, and Knepp Park, home to Tamworth pigs, longhorn cattle and Exmoor ponies. If the countryside all around looks like a tidy, landscaped park, then the park itself looks increasingly unkempt as the livestock graze and biodiversity increases. All in all, urbanity in the smart houses, rusticity in the remote farms, fantasy in the old remains, felicity in the autumn colours.
The sights:
Christ's Hospital:
An independent school founded for poor boys by Edward VI in 1553, but moved from the City of London to Sussex in the C19. Around 900 girls and boys (whose education is still paid for by bursaries) who wear Tudor-style uniforms of dark blue serge with yellow stockings. Main buildings are huge and in a simplified Gothic-Elizabethan style by Aston Webb, begun 1893, finished 1902.
West Grinstead:
The topographer Ian Nairn is worth quoting: 'Halfway between Horsham and the Downs, at a point where the Weald has opened out and become more park-like, with trim hedges rather than copses. The Burrells with their pair of Nash houses [Knepp Castle and West Grinstead Park] and attendant landscaping have given it a character unlike anywhere else in Sussex: The Weald has been at first tamed, then let back, on a leash as it were, to be wild within limits.' Gateland's Farm is C17, Grade II-listed, gabled, tiled and timber-framed but with an alarmingly leaning chimney. St George's Church is by the River Adur and has stone slab roofs and a low, shingled spire. Early Norman north aisle, the rest is C13 but with a C15 timber porch. Good monuments such as brasses and busts by Rysbrack and Flaxman. Glebe Cottage is C18 and Glebe House is c1600. West Grinstead Station was on the Beeching-cut Horsham-Shoreham line and retains platforms, signage, signals and a British Railways Mark 1 carriage in green Southern livery.
Knepp Estate:
Old Knepp Castle is a fragment of an C11 century Norman keep, 10m tall, with a mound and a small motte. New Knepp Castle was built by John Nash in 1809. Stucco, not stone, and in a flamboyant and irregular design. Burnt in 1904 and rebuilt exactly. Park by Humphrey Repton. The website states about the estate:
'
3,500 acres in the heart of the Sussex Weald. Knepp Estate...has been owned by the Burrells for over 220 years...Until recently most of the land was devoted to traditional arable and dairy farming but in 2001 we shifted our focus entirely and embarked on a series of regeneration and restoration projects aimed at nature conservation - or 'rewilding', as it has come to be known. We are still farming, just in a less intensive way - producing organic, pasture-fed meat from free-roaming herds of animals within the Wildland project.' We'll mostly just see the parkland.
Dragon's Green:
A hamlet of pretty weatherboarded and timber-framed cottages but also some 1950s houses which give a suburban feel. The George and Dragon Pub is very pleasant. Handsome Newbuildings Place is 'Artisan Mannerist' in style, dated 1683, stone and brick built with a Dutch gable and home to Wilfred Scawen Blunt, author, poet, traveller and breeder of Arab horses, who is buried in the grounds.
Dogs:
I love having dogs on my walks and this walk is suitable for them. It is of moderate length, but there will be fields with livestock and a number of stiles and roads to negotiate. A dog must be obedient if it is off the lead.
The
route
(please click the link in red to see it and note that if the autumn has been very wet, much of the route will be switched to tarmac lanes):
Setting off in a southerly then southeasterly direction we'll take the Downs Link former railway line and cycle path to Southwater and eventually to West Grinstead Station. Heading southwest along Park Lane we'll reach West Grinstead hamlet where we'll cross the River Adur and then, heading east, the A24. Routes through the Knepp Estate will enable us to pick up a bridleway will take us north past Green Street to the lane to Dragon's Green. A route west than northwest, then north along a lane will head back past Netherwood and Lawson's Farm to the cycle path which will return us, via the outward-bound route, back to the station.

Title: The Enchanted Forest Light Show
Summary:
By day, Faskally Forest near Pitlochry is a beautiful array of mixed woodland with some very tall trees indeed. It has lochans and a network of paths to entice you into the forest's depths.
For about 4 weeks a year, as the sun gets low in the sky, and when we put the clocks back, the forest is transformed by a mesmerising and interactive light show that blows your mind, "How have they come up with that?" It's not just about lights, it's about how they (a) mesmerise and (b) with narration educate about the importance of life in our forests for just about every other form of life on the planet.
WHEN?
OutdoorLads will be going on Sunday 1st November, 5.30pm. We're likely to be inside the forest for up to two hours. Clocks go back before then, sunset will be 4.30, so properly dark by 5.30.
WHAT'S THE PLAN?
Most importantly,
YOU HAVE TO PURCHASE YOUR OWN ENTRANCE TICKET
Signing up to the event page alone does not get you in. The ticket prices are about £40 but there are some concessions available.
Buy your ticket for Sunday 1st November, 17.30 slot. If this fills, you could buy for the slots either side and meet the rest of us inside.
The ticket includes coach travel from the centre of Pitlochry (close to the railway station) - you cannot gain access in your own vehicle. It includes the return of course.
WHAT ELSE MIGHT WE DO ON THE DAY?
Nearer the time, we'll see who's going and try to fix up a Sunday lunch for those who can get there early afternoon. Pitlochry is a lovely town with lots to see and do including local walks, shops, places to eat and drink.
If you're travelling by public transport, Pitlochry is well connected by rail and coach services with Ember, Citylink and Flixbus. Check engineering works that might affect Sunday and especially late Sunday trains.
This event is not suitable for dogs.

Title: The Weekend Gathering
Summary:
Scottish Leaders  - this weekend is just for you!
In a change to our usual routine of biannual meetings, we've blown the budget by booking a comfortable hostel for a couple of nights, which is heavily subsidised by OutdoorLads.
It's a chance to celebrate the organisation, our positive impact on our community and how volunteers make it happen. A chance to connect and network with other leaders, share ideas and tips, inspiration, motivation and plans. It's also a thank you from OutdoorLads to you for all you put into the organisation, without which - there would be no OutdoorLads! But don't worry - this IS NOT a whole weekend of Alan droning on about how last month had three more attendees than last year.... we'll also be getting outside, partaking in activities and getting to know each other!
We are planning to make full use of the weekend - Friday evening will be an opportunity to socialise with most of the rest of the Scottish leader team; Saturday will be a full mixed day discussing challenges and opportunities while also getting out for a walk and talk; and we may have a short session on Sunday morning before heading home.
This weekend is aimed at leaders in Scotland, should space become available leaders from elsewhere who were unable to attend the similar events we ran in February and March 2026 are also welcome to attend, especially those based in the far north of England.
To note:
This event is heavily subsidised by OutdoorLads, and food is provided over the weekend. Travel expenses are not provided for this event. If that cost is a struggle for you, we don't want that to be a reason for you not to join us - please apply to the
OutdoorLads Foundation
for help with that cost.
Although the standard refund policy applies to this event, if you need to cancel, please do so as early as possible, so we can ensure the event is as full as possible with leaders who can benefit from the weekend.
If you are not yet a leader you will need to have applied and be well on with your leader application to join this event. If you're not sure if you should book or not, drop the office a line on
support@outdoorlads.com
and we'll chat it through with you. We will remove any bookings from members who are not leaders and haven't got an active leader application in.

Title: Fireside evenings above the Calder Valley
Summary:
A weekend retreat to remember!
Perched high above the Calder Valley, this 17th‑century Grade II listed camping barn has a real off‑the‑beaten‑track feel, surrounded by open countryside and wide Pennine views. It’s a perfect place to experience the autumn leaves and the breezes that sweep across the rolling hills.
From the barn, there are many options for nearby walks include the dramatic ridge to Stoodley Pike, loops around local reservoirs, or gentler valley walks towards Hebden Bridge and Hardcastle Crags. For those wanting something lower level, there are plenty of scenic paths straight from the door. If you’re not walking, you can head into Todmorden or Hebden Bridge for cafés, shops and a slower day, or settle in for a reading day in the large indoor activity space.
This event is a two‑night weekend retreat. Walks will take place on Saturday, with routes chosen closer to the time based on weather. It’s also a great opportunity to get involved in route planning if you’d like to contribute.
Accommodation
The barn is simple, but we’ll create fantastic memories through community, conversation and cosy fireside moments. This peaceful rural setting is a great way to experience the wilder side of West Yorkshire. Expect a couple of days of walking, cooking together and being part of a friendly, welcoming group.
Accommodation is in shared bunk‑bed rooms. No bedding is provided – you MUST bring your own sleeping bag, bedding and pillow.
We’ve got access to a well‑equipped kitchen with fridge/freezer, a lounge area, an accessible wet‑room shower, toilet blocks, and a large indoor barn space for activities. Wi‑Fi is available.
Heating is provided by wood‑pellet and multifuel stoves, and there’s also an outdoor fire pit and campfire area for relaxed evenings.
Food
Friday night will be a buffet – please bring something to share. Saturday night will be a shared meal cooked by the leader, with breakfast included on both Saturday and Sunday mornings.
Dogs:
This event is not suitable for dogs.
If this is your first OutdoorLads event:
If this is your first event, we’ll make sure you feel welcomed. Please
check out the My First Hostel page
, and don’t hesitate to drop me a message if you have questions.

Title: Halloween at Dunster: Castles, Coast, and Celtic Hills
Summary:
Join us for a fantastic, varied Halloween day walk exploring the dramatic landscapes surrounding the historic medieval village of Dunster. This is a relatively short, circular route packed with diverse scenery—taking us from ancient wooded hills and historic settlements to the sweeping Somerset coastline, before tracking the nostalgic West Somerset Railway.
We’ll finish with plenty of time to spare in the afternoon to explore the magnificent Dunster Castle and its gorgeous gardens. Costumes are entirely optional, but a bit of Halloween spirit is highly encouraged!
Event Overview
Date:
Saturday, 31st October 2026
Duration:
Approximately 4 hours (excluding castle visit)
Distance:
Around 8.5 miles (13.5 km)
Difficulty:
Moderate. A few steady climbs into the hills, but well-paced with plenty of flat coastal walking to balance it out.
The Route
We begin our journey in the shadow of Dunster Castle, heading straight out into the atmospheric autumnal canopy of Dunster Park.
The Highs:
We’ll climb steadily up through the woods towards the ancient iron-age hillforts of
Bat’s Castle
and
Black Ball
, offering spectacular, moody views over the surrounding Somerset landscape and the Bristol Channel.
The Valleys & Villages:
Skirting the ridges of Aller Hill and Withycombe Hill, we'll drop down through the quiet combes and charming villages of Withycombe and Carhampton.
The Coast:
From Carhampton, we head north to meet the coast at
Blue Anchor
. Here, we'll grab some fresh sea air and look out across the waves.
The Rails:
The final leg brings us back west, tracking alongside the historic
West Somerset Railway
line and crossing the flat marshlands straight back into Dunster.
Afternoon: Dunster Castle & Gardens
After wrapping up the walk, the afternoon is yours to enjoy. We will head over to Dunster Castle (managed by the National Trust). Perched dramatically on a tor, this ancient fortress turned grand country house is the perfect setting for a Halloween afternoon.
You can wander through the multi-tiered subtropical gardens, explore the historic mill, or head inside the castle to soak up centuries of history (and perhaps a ghost story or two).
> Note: National Trust members get into the castle and gardens for free, so remember to bring your membership card! Non-members can purchase tickets on the day.
A Few Haunted Highlights... 🕷️
Dunster has a reputation for being one of the most active paranormal hotspots in the country—local lore says nearly every historic building in the village has a resident spirit. The castle itself has been investigated by the National Trust for its eerie occurrences. Keep an eye out for:
The Grey Lady:
Dunster’s most famous resident spectre, she is frequently seen gliding majestically down the grand 17th-century oak staircase before completely vanishing into a solid wall.
The Man in Green:
If you pop into the National Trust gift shop (housed in the old 17th-century stable block), you might spot a mysterious figure dressed head-to-toe in green walking calmly through the building before disappearing into thin air.
The Chinking of Coins:
On certain days, the ghostly sound of money being counted echoes near the old keeps. Local legend attributes this to the infamous William de Mohun ("The Scourge of the West"), who minted his own illegal currency here during the medieval Civil War.
The Foot of the Blue Kitchen:
In one of the modernised volunteer areas known as the Blue Kitchen, a shaken worker once reported a completely disembodied, naked human foot appearing out of nowhere on the floor before dissolving.
The Seven-Foot Skeleton:
Deep beneath the Gatehouse dungeon, archaeologists once uncovered the remains of a prisoner standing over seven feet tall, still shackled by his wrists and ankles to the stone wall. While no specific ghost has been spotted, visitors note a distinct drop in temperature, and dogs notoriously refuse to go near the steps leading down to it.
Even on our walk before we reach the castle, keep your ears open—tourists on the nearby hills have previously reported the distinct, booming sound of a massive troop of soldiers marching past them, despite the hillsides being completely empty!
If you want to get a little extra Spooky, Dunster Castle is running Ghost Tours after dark when the castle is closed to the public on Halloween.  It's £25 a ticket and I've booked myself onto the 7pm tour.  If you want to join me, you can book a ticket here:
https://www.nationaltrust-tickets.org.uk/event-tickets/34525?
What to Bring
Footwear:
Sturdy walking boots or muddy-trail shoes are highly recommended, as the woodland and hill paths can be damp and slick in late October.
Clothing:
Layer up for autumn weather and bring a reliable waterproof jacket—the coastal stretch can get breezy!
Food & Drink:
Pack a packed lunch, snacks, and plenty of water for the trail. We will find a scenic spot along the hills or coast for a lunch stop.
Money/Card:
For entry to the Castle/Gardens if you aren't an NT member, or for a well-deserved hot drink/pint in Dunster afterwards.
Dogs
Dogs are welcome to join us on this event but we do ask the following:
Please appreciate the fact that not everyone is a dog owner or lover- especially when we stop to eat
Please ensure you adhere to the Countryside Code at all times - see (
Keeping Dogs Under Effective Control)
If your dog is uncontrolled and strays in open land frightening other animals or livestock, the leader is supported by the OutdoorLads board of trustees to ask you to leave the event as this is not acceptable behaviour.
